A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AFEG research work. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable, allowing relocated material to be matched reliably.

before.justification: Sections 4 and Appendix C report original policy simulations on synthetic graphs and ICPSR disease networks, including detection rewards and computational timings.

after.justification: Sections 4 and Appendix C retain original synthetic and disease-network simulations and add experiments using noisy probability distributions.

M1.justification: The Gittins recursion, maximum-index frontier selection, BFS tree heuristic, shared-parameter MRF, and pseudolikelihood learning procedure remain unchanged. Algorithm 1's expanded computation lines and the worked example document the existing method.

E1.justification: The synthetic tree/non-tree tasks and all five ICPSR disease domains remain. Section 4.3.1 adds a distinct scenario in which policies receive a noisy probability model while outcomes follow the underlying model. Changed network sizes concern sampling within retained coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding synthetic and disease comparisons retain Random, Greedy, and DQN, with Optimal restricted to small synthetic instances. The noisy-model experiments use existing comparators. The newly discussed Meister–Kleinberg work is not evaluated as a baseline.

E3.justification: Disease evaluation switches from discounted/undiscounted reward totals to fraction-detected curves and uses revised graph instances. Reported full HIV and syphilis networks change from 643 and 409 nodes to 778 and 542; subsamples also change, and full-network evaluations disappear. A new protocol perturbs model parameters at five noise levels. The disease discount factor and 200 Monte Carlo rollouts remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 4.3.1 and Figures 6/14 add systematic sensitivity tests of inaccurate probability models across all five diseases: decisions use Qε while outcomes follow P. This supplies empirical robustness evidence absent from v1, which already contained a theoretical misspecification bound. The synthetic edge-addition analysis remains.

E5.justification: V2 newly reports standard errors across ten noisy-model instantiations per noise level. V1's reporting of three independently sampled disease subgraphs with seeds {0,1,2}, and their separate panels, disappears. These are different sources of replication, not an increase from three to ten runs of the same experiment.

E6.justification: Disease outcome curves and timings are revised, and noisy-model results are added. For example, Figure 5 reports HIV Gittins setup times of 29 versus 24 seconds and Greedy rollout times of 272 versus 840 seconds, on different subsamples; these are not same-setting performance changes. V1's three-subsample and full-network result collections are not retained.

T1.justification: New Appendix A.3 introduces changepoint notation, Observation 7, and Lemma 8 with an inductive bound of 1 + |Ω| times the number of descendants. Theorem 6 now invokes this lemma instead of its earlier brief counting argument. The existing forest-optimality, parameter-gradient, and model-misspecification results are retained.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same headline claims: forest optimality, polynomial-time index computation, strong performance beyond trees, and nearly complete HIV detection when testing half the population. Additional evidence does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: V2 attributes noisy-model degradation to reduced information about P, explains choosing BFS trees to limit artificial frontier restrictions, and explicitly acknowledges high-degree nodes in sexual networks. Existing limitations concerning fixed graphs, inference costs, and tree-only guarantees remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A explains representing piecewise functions through changepoints, slopes, and intercepts. Section 4.3.1 specifies parameter perturbations, and Figure 5 explicitly states that policy training occurs once for all 200 rollouts. Hardware, repository access, and data-access disclosures remain substantively unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds four references: Meister–Kleinberg on contact-tracing order and three studies supporting sparse or tree-like transmission networks. Section 2 distinguishes the known-root infection process of Meister–Kleinberg from AFEG's jointly distributed statuses. The broader research positioning remains intact.

P1.justification: V2 adds sustained worked-example exposition, reorganizes Section 4.3 and Appendix C.4, and changes the appendix sequence from application/proofs/experiments to worked example/application/experiments/proofs. Much introductory and concluding prose remains unchanged; label notation changes from Σ to Ω.

P2.justification: Figure 5 is redesigned around five normalized disease plots and a consolidated timing table. New worked-example and noise figures accompany removal of the earlier extensive disease panels; tables are relocated and expanded. Figure 3 selects different existing synthetic panels, matching the stated β = 0.9 focus.

improvement.justification: Noisy-model tests and expanded explanations add value, but v2 removes the three-subsample and full-network evidence and changes network statistics without explaining why. The new worked example also introduces an inconsistency: Appendix A.2's large-m formula gives Φ(10) > 10, contradicting Eq. (2). Gains in coverage and exposition therefore coexist with losses in empirical transparency and mathematical clarity, preventing a reliable net-quality judgment.
